definition: A departure from what is normal or expected; an anomaly.
context_sentences: The minister described the corruption as an aberration, not the norm.
Scientists recorded an aberration in the climate data from the Niger Delta.
etymology: From Latin aberrare — to wander away

definition: Hostile and aggressive; engaged in a war or conflict.
context_sentences: The belligerent tone of the speech alarmed the peace delegates.
A belligerent attitude never resolves disputes — dialogue does.
etymology: From Latin belligerare — to wage war

definition: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds.
context_sentences: The cacophony of Lagos traffic at rush hour is unlike anything else.
The debate descended into a cacophony of shouting and accusations.

definition: In a state of disrepair or ruin due to neglect.
context_sentences: The dilapidated school building had no roof left after the rainy season.
Many dilapidated hospitals in rural areas lack basic medical equipment.
etymology: From Latin dilapidare — to scatter like stones

definition: Lasting for only a very short time; transitory.
context_sentences: Social media fame is often ephemeral — here today, forgotten tomorrow.
Beauty is ephemeral, but the impact of good character lasts forever.
etymology: From Greek ephemeros — lasting only a day

definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; very concerned about cleanliness.
context_sentences: The fastidious editor corrected every comma in the student's essay.
Her fastidious attention to hygiene earned her praise from the school nurse.

definition: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters.
context_sentences: The garrulous market woman had a story for every customer who passed.
His garrulous nature made meetings run over time every single week.

definition: Leadership or dominance, especially of one country or social group over others.
context_sentences: Nigeria's cultural hegemony in West Africa is reflected in its music and film.
Economic hegemony does not always translate into the welfare of ordinary people.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of an individual's peculiar behaviour or way of thinking.
context_sentences: His idiosyncratic teaching style confused students at first but proved effective.
The idiosyncratic naming traditions of the Yoruba reflect their deep spirituality.

definition: The fact of placing two things close together for contrasting effect.
context_sentences: The juxtaposition of wealth and poverty on Lagos Island tells a powerful story.
Achebe's juxtaposition of tradition and modernity drives the conflict in 'Things Fall Apart'.

definition: Tearful or given to weeping; inducing tears.
context_sentences: The lachrymose ending of the play moved every student in the audience.
She became lachrymose whenever she recalled her years of hardship before success.

definition: Very generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful.
context_sentences: The magnanimous victor offered the defeated team words of genuine encouragement.
A magnanimous leader forgives past wrongs for the sake of national unity.

definition: Wicked and criminal; morally wrong in a scandalous way.
context_sentences: The nefarious activities of corrupt officials rob the nation of its future.
In literature, the villain's nefarious schemes are usually exposed by the hero.

definition: Characterized by a showy display intended to impress; pretentious.
context_sentences: The ostentatious party was widely criticized as an insult to the poor.
Ostentatious wealth without corresponding humility is frowned upon in many Nigerian cultures.

definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way.
context_sentences: Drug abuse has a pernicious influence on young people's academic performance.
Fake news spreads pernicious misinformation that can destroy communities.

definition: Exceedingly idealistic; unrealistic and impractical.
context_sentences: His quixotic dream of ending corruption overnight ignored the depth of the problem.
The reformer was called quixotic, yet history proved his ideals were right.
etymology: From Don Quixote, the idealistic character by Cervantes

definition: Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude toward authority.
context_sentences: The recalcitrant student refused to apologize despite the teacher's patience.
Some recalcitrant officials refused to implement the new transparency policies.
etymology: From Latin recalcitrare — to kick back

definition: A person who tries to gain favour through flattery and excessive agreement.
context_sentences: The politician surrounded himself with sycophants who told him only what he wanted to hear.
A true friend speaks the truth; a sycophant only praises to gain favour.

definition: The action of evading clear commitment to a definite course of action; equivocation.
context_sentences: The senator's tergiversation on the bill frustrated his constituents.
Tergiversation in leadership erodes public trust faster than outright failure.
etymology: From Latin tergiversari — to turn one's back

definition: Offence or annoyance; the feeling of being insulted.
context_sentences: She took great umbrage at the suggestion that she had cheated.
The delegation took umbrage at the disrespectful tone of the negotiations.

definition: Expressing opinions or complaints loudly and forcefully.
context_sentences: The vociferous protest outside the National Assembly lasted three days.
Human rights activists are vociferous in demanding justice for the oppressed.

definition: Deliberately cruel or harmful without reason; unrestrained.
context_sentences: The wanton destruction of school property is a criminal offence.
There is no justification for the wanton abuse of human rights.

definition: Intense dislike or fear of people from other countries or cultures.
context_sentences: Xenophobia tears apart communities that could benefit from cultural exchange.
The WAEC essay required students to discuss the causes of xenophobia in Africa.

definition: Fanatical and uncompromising pursuit of ideals; extreme devotion to a cause.
context_sentences: Religious zealotry has been the source of conflicts throughout human history.
There is a fine line between passionate belief and dangerous zealotry.
etymology: From Greek zelotes — one who is jealous or zealous

definition: Bitterness or ill feeling in speech or manner.
context_sentences: The acrimony between the two political parties made governance impossible.
She expressed her disappointment without acrimony, only quiet sadness.

definition: Using high-sounding language with little real meaning; inflated.
context_sentences: His bombastic speech impressed no one who understood the real issues at hand.
Good writers avoid bombastic language and prefer clarity over complexity.
etymology: From Greek bombyx — cotton padding (stuffed speech)

definition: Given to sudden changes of mood or behaviour; unpredictable.
context_sentences: The capricious policy changes made it impossible for businesses to plan.
A capricious leader cannot build the stable institutions a nation needs.
etymology: From Italian capriccio — a sudden start, whim

definition: Excessively harsh or severe, especially with regard to laws or punishment.
context_sentences: The draconian law imposed a curfew that violated citizens' basic freedoms.
Human rights groups protested the draconian penalties for minor offences.
etymology: From Draco, the ancient Athenian lawmaker known for harsh laws

definition: To use ambiguous language to avoid commitment or to mislead.
context_sentences: The official tried to equivocate when questioned about the missing funds.
A person of integrity does not equivocate — they speak plainly and honestly.
etymology: From Latin aequivocus — of equal voice, ambiguous

definition: The obstruction of legislation by prolonged speechmaking.
context_sentences: The opposition senator staged a filibuster that delayed the vote for six hours.
A filibuster is a tactic used to prevent a bill from being passed into law.

definition: Fond of company; sociable; living in flocks or communities.
context_sentences: Her gregarious personality made her the most popular student in the school.
Humans are gregarious by nature — we thrive in communities.

definition: A lengthy and aggressive speech; to lecture someone at length.
context_sentences: The principal's harangue about punctuality lasted the entire assembly period.
He harangued his team after the loss, which only decreased their morale.
etymology: From Old French harangue — public speech

definition: Exemption from punishment or freedom from the consequences of an action.
context_sentences: Corruption thrives when officials act with impunity and face no consequences.
The rule of law ensures that no one can break the law with impunity.
etymology: From Latin impunitas — freedom from punishment

definition: A government in which leaders use political power to steal their country's resources.
context_sentences: The essay argued that kleptocracy, not poverty, is Africa's greatest curse.
Citizens must demand accountability to prevent their nation from becoming a kleptocracy.

definition: Excessively ready to use legal proceedings to settle disputes.
context_sentences: The litigious nature of the business dispute clogged up the court system.
A litigious society can sometimes stifle progress through endless legal battles.
etymology: From Latin litigiosus — fond of disputes

definition: Wrongdoing, especially by a public official.
context_sentences: The governor was impeached for malfeasance in the management of public funds.
Malfeasance in office is a serious charge that can end a political career.

definition: The practice of favouring relatives or close friends in employment, regardless of merit.
context_sentences: Nepotism in public service appointments denies qualified candidates their chance.
The committee investigated allegations of nepotism in the scholarship awards.
etymology: From Italian nipote — nephew (originally referring to popes favouring nephews)

definition: Obedient or attentive to an excessive or servile degree.
context_sentences: The obsequious aide agreed with everything the director said, however wrong.
Genuine respect is different from obsequious flattery — one builds, the other corrodes.

definition: Deceitful and untrustworthy; guilty of betrayal.
context_sentences: The perfidious ally signed the peace treaty and then broke it within weeks.
History remembers perfidious leaders who betrayed the trust of their people.

definition: Complaining in a petulant or whining manner.
context_sentences: The querulous passenger complained about every detail of the journey.
A querulous attitude alienates friends and closes doors that patience would open.

definition: The art of effective and persuasive speaking or writing; language designed to persuade.
context_sentences: The candidate's inspiring rhetoric won over many undecided voters.
Empty rhetoric without action is one of the hallmarks of poor leadership.
etymology: From Greek rhetorike — art of the orator

definition: Inciting or causing people to rebel against the authority of a state.
context_sentences: The government declared the pamphlets seditious and ordered them confiscated.
Freedom of speech does not protect seditious material that incites violence.
etymology: From Latin seditio — going apart, revolt

definition: Eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant.
context_sentences: The truculent defendant interrupted the proceedings multiple times.
A truculent negotiator often achieves less than a measured and calm one.

definition: A change of circumstances or fortune, typically for the worse; ups and downs.
context_sentences: Nigeria's history is marked by the vicissitudes of military rule and democracy.
Through every vicissitude, the resilient people rebuilt their lives and communities.

definition: Using high-flown or bombastic language; grandiloquent.
context_sentences: The magniloquent speech was impressive in delivery but shallow in substance.
Writers are warned against magniloquent prose that prioritises sound over sense.

definition: Having a ready insight into things; shrewd and discerning.
context_sentences: A perspicacious student recognises the deeper themes beneath a poem's surface.
Her perspicacious analysis of the budget revealed hidden inconsistencies.

definition: Expressing or promoting a particular cause or point of view; biased.
context_sentences: The tendentious newspaper article ignored all evidence that contradicted its thesis.
Academic writing should be objective, not tendentious or politically motivated.
etymology: From Latin tendere — to stretch, aim

definition: The appearance of being true or real; believable realism in a narrative.
context_sentences: Chinua Achebe's descriptions of Igbo village life give his fiction remarkable verisimilitude.
Good historical fiction balances invention with verisimilitude to feel authentic.

definition: Showing a lack of courage or determination; timid and cowardly.
context_sentences: The pusillanimous minister refused to speak out against the unjust policy.
History does not remember pusillanimous leaders — it remembers the courageous ones.

definition: The use of many words where fewer would do; the use of indirect expression.
context_sentences: Politicians are notorious for using circumlocution to avoid direct answers.
Good writing replaces circumlocution with precise, clear, and direct language.

definition: A state of temporary disuse or suspension.
context_sentences: The reconstruction of the bridge in Abuja was held in abeyance during the heavy rain.
The contract disputes put all further investments in abeyance.
etymology: From Old French abeiance — expectation, suspension

definition: Repeal or do away with (a law, right, or formal agreement).
context_sentences: The senate voted to abrogate the outdated trade agreement with neighboring countries.
A constitutional amendment was passed to abrogate the decree.
etymology: From Latin abrogare — to repeal, abolish

definition: Difficult to understand; obscure.
context_sentences: The professor's lecture on economic theory was too abstruse for the freshers.
She preferred clear explanations over abstruse philosophical debates.
etymology: From Latin abstrudere — to conceal, hide away

definition: An award or privilege granted as a special honour or as an acknowledgment of merit.
context_sentences: The writer received the highest national accolade for her contributions to African literature.
Every student who scored straight A's in WAEC was honored with an accolade.
etymology: From French accolade — a hug or embrace on receiving knighthood

definition: Accept something reluctantly but without protest.
context_sentences: The community refused to acquiesce to the displacement caused by the oil refinery.
Faced with overwhelming evidence, the suspect had no choice but to acquiesce to the terms.
etymology: From Latin acquiescere — to find rest, remain quiet

definition: Make a formal judgment on a disputed matter.
context_sentences: A special panel was set up in Enugu to adjudicate land ownership disputes.
The committee is authorized to adjudicate all student disciplinary issues.
etymology: From Latin adjudicare — to award by judicial decision

definition: Excessive admiration or praise.
context_sentences: The music superstar was greeted with loud adulation by fans at the Lagos airport.
True leaders seek honest feedback rather than the adulation of crowd followers.

definition: Friendly, good-natured, or easy to talk to.
context_sentences: The new principal was an affable man who greeted students warmly every morning.
Her affable demeanor made her well-liked among customers at the marketplace.
etymology: From Latin affabilis — easy to speak to

definition: Brisk and cheerful readiness.
context_sentences: The class captain accepted the assignment with alacrity and finished it in an hour.
The emergency response team rushed to the scene with impressive alacrity.

definition: Loyalty or commitment of a subordinate to a superior or of an individual to a group or cause.
context_sentences: Nigerian citizens pledge their allegiance to the nation during morning assembly.
The soldiers swore a solemn oath of allegiance to defend the republic.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman French ligeance — relationship of a vassal to a lord

definition: A noisy argument or disagreement, especially in public.
context_sentences: A minor traffic altercation on Third Mainland Bridge caused a long delay.
The discussion devolved into an altercation and had to be dismissed.

definition: Exceptionally pleasing to taste or smell; especially delicious or fragrant.
context_sentences: The kitchen was filled with the ambrosial aroma of freshly baked jollof rice.
She prepared an ambrosial feast to welcome the elders back to the village.
etymology: From Greek ambrosios — belonging to the gods, immortal

definition: Destroy utterly; obliterate.
context_sentences: A powerful pesticide was used to annihilate the locust invasion on the farm.
The storms threaten to annihilate the weak coastal settlements along the shore.
etymology: From Latin annihilare — to reduce to nothing

definition: The condition of being anonymous.
context_sentences: The philanthropist requested absolute anonymity when donating the new library.
Online anonymity can sometimes lead to irresponsible behavior on forums.

definition: A deep-seated feeling of aversion or dislike.
context_sentences: There is a natural antipathy between the traditional rivals in the spelling league.
His antipathy toward cold weather made him prefer staying indoors all winter.

definition: A person or thing that is the direct opposite of someone or something else.
context_sentences: His selfish actions are the exact antithesis of the school's moral code.
Her calm response stood in direct antithesis to her brother's angry outburst.
etymology: From Greek antithesis — opposition, setting against

definition: The complete final destruction of the world, or a monumental disaster.
context_sentences: The farmers feared an economic apocalypse if the drought continued for another month.
The movie portrayed a post-apocalypse world where resources were scarce.

definition: The highest point in the development of something; a climax or culmination.
context_sentences: The empire reached its apogee during the golden era of trade and expansion.
Winning the international award was the absolute apogee of the scientist's career.
etymology: From Greek apogaion — away from the earth

definition: A person who prepared and sold medicines and drugs (historical).
context_sentences: The sick traveler went to the village apothecary to buy a herbal remedy.
Before modern drugstores, the local apothecary prepared all cures by hand.

definition: Based on random choice or personal whim, rather than any reason or system.
context_sentences: The teacher's arbitrary division of project groups frustrated the class.
Laws must be based on clear principles rather than arbitrary decisions by rulers.
etymology: From Latin registrarius — depending on an arbiter

definition: A very typical example of a certain person or thing; an original that has been imitated.
context_sentences: Achebe's Okonkwo has become the archetype of a tragic traditional leader.
The builder designed the new houses based on a classic archetype.

definition: Showing great care and perseverance.
context_sentences: Through assiduous preparation, the student scored straight A's in the exams.
The research required months of assiduous work in the laboratories.
etymology: From Latin assiduus — sitting down to, busy

definition: Showing a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks.
context_sentences: The entrepreneur launched an audacious plan to build affordable solar power stations in rural areas.
It was an audacious rescue mission that saved the trapped miners.

definition: Severe or strict in manner, attitude, or appearance; simple and without comfort.
context_sentences: The monks lived an austere life in the desert, dedicated purely to study.
The minimalist living room had an austere beauty with very little decoration.
etymology: From Greek austeros — harsh, bitter, dry

definition: A sudden arrival of a large number of something; a mass of snow/ice falling down a mountain.
context_sentences: The customer service desk received an avalanche of complaints after the power outage.
Skiers were warned to stay off the steep slopes due to the risk of an avalanche.
etymology: From French avalanche — descent of snow, landslip

definition: Extreme greed for wealth or material gain.
context_sentences: The novel depicts how the banker's avarice eventually led to his downfall.
Public resources must be protected from the avarice of corrupt officials.

definition: So lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring.
context_sentences: The pop song had a banal melody and repetitive lyrics that tired listeners.

etymology: From French banal — belonging to a feudal lord, common to all

definition: Highly ornate and extravagant in style.
context_sentences: The cathedral's baroque architecture featured gold carvings and elaborate murals.
His baroque writing style was full of complex metaphors and long adjectives.
etymology: From Portuguese barroco — irregular or misshapen pearl

definition: A huge or monstrous creature, or something enormous.
context_sentences: The telecommunications company became a global behemoth after the merger.
In the ancient legend, a giant behemoth guarded the entrance to the forest.

definition: An indicator or predictor of the path of a trend.
context_sentences: Lagos is often considered the economic bellwether of the West African subregion.
The performance of the tech stocks is a bellwether for the entire market.
etymology: From Middle English bellewether — leading sheep wearing a bell

definition: Generous or doing good.
context_sentences: A beneficent community leader built a water borehole for the market women.
The foundation's beneficent donations supported free education for orphans.

definition: Surrounded by armed forces aiming to capture it; overwhelmed by requests/questions.
context_sentences: The customer care agent was besieged with complaints during the system upgrade.
The ancient fortress was besieged for three months before the garrison surrendered.
etymology: From Middle English besegen — to sit down around a place

definition: Damage the reputation of (someone or something) in the opinion of others.
context_sentences: He filed a lawsuit against the newspaper for trying to besmirch his family name.
A politician's rivals will often spread rumors to besmirch their integrity.
etymology: From English be- + smirch — to make dirty or soil

definition: Formal agreement to marry; engagement.
context_sentences: The families gathered in Calabar to celebrate the traditional betrothal ceremony.
In the historical story, the betrothal of the prince sealed the peace treaty.
etymology: From Middle English betrouthen — to pledge truth or engage

definition: (of a legislative body) having two branches or chambers.
context_sentences: Nigeria has a bicameral legislature consisting of the Senate and House of Representatives.
A bicameral parliament ensures that bills undergo dual levels of scrutiny.

definition: A small baked cake, typically crisp, flat, and sweet.
context_sentences: The child dipped a sweet biscuit into a warm cup of cocoa.
She served tea and a ginger biscuit to the guests in the parlour.

definition: (of bad behaviour) done openly and unashamedly.
context_sentences: The student's blatant copying during the test earned him immediate suspension.
Refusing to yield right of way to an ambulance is a blatant violation of rules.

definition: Socially unconventional in an artistic way.
context_sentences: The art gallery in Yaba attracted writers who lived a bohemian lifestyle.

definition: An attractively arranged bunch of flowers, or the characteristic scent of a wine or perfume.
context_sentences: The bride carried a beautiful bouquet of roses and lilies down the aisle.
The rich bouquet of coffee beans filled the roastery with a warm aroma.
etymology: From Old French bosquet — little wood, cluster of trees

definition: A bold manner or a show of boldness intended to impress or intimidate.
context_sentences: His tough talk was mere bravado to hide his underlying nervousness.
The goalkeeper faced the penalty shooter with a displays of silent bravado.

definition: A small book or magazine containing pictures and information about a product or service.
context_sentences: The school registrar handed a colorful admission brochure to the visiting parent.
The travel agent gave us a brochure detailing tours in Nigeria's national parks.
etymology: From French brocher — to sew or stitch (stitched booklet)

definition: The ability or tendency to float in a fluid; optimism or cheerfulness.
context_sentences: The high salt content of the water increases the buoyancy of swimmers.
Her natural buoyancy and positive attitude kept the team motivated during the crisis.

definition: An office or department for transacting particular business; a writing desk with drawers.
context_sentences: The National Bureau of Statistics published the new employment data yesterday.
He stored the family records in the top drawer of the antique bureau.
etymology: From French bureau — office desk (originally coarse woolen cloth used to cover writing tables)

definition: A modulation or inflection of the voice; rhythmic flow of a sequence of words.
context_sentences: The poet recited her verses with a musical cadence that charmed the audience.
The steady cadence of the gangan drum set the pace for the dancers.

definition: A chemical stimulant found in tea and coffee plants.
context_sentences: Drinking coffee late at night keeps you awake due to its high caffeine content.
Many students rely on caffeine to study through the night during exam week.
etymology: From German Kaffein — derived from coffee (Kaffee)

definition: An evergreen tropical American tree, or the hollow gourd fruit used as a container.
context_sentences: The elder drank fresh palm wine from a beautifully carved calabash.
Traditional musicians use a beaded calabash as a percussion instrument.

definition: Gymnastic exercises to achieve bodily fitness and grace of movement.
context_sentences: Every morning before classes, the boarders gathered for calisthenics on the field.
You don't need heavy gym equipment if you perform calisthenics regularly.

definition: (of a young person) inexperienced and immature.
context_sentences: The callow youth thought he knew more than the elders who had lived for decades.
A callow attitude in leadership can lead to costly errors in governance.
etymology: From Old English calu — bald, featherless (young birds)

definition: Work in an organized and active way toward a particular goal, typically political or social.
context_sentences: The Ministry of Health launched a nationwide campaign to vaccinate children.
The students started a campaign to clean up the school grounds after exams.
etymology: From Latin campania — open country, battlefield

definition: A large branched holder for several candles or lamps.
context_sentences: The dining table in the palace was decorated with a silver candelabrum.
During the power cut, they lit a candelabrum to illuminate the entire hall.
